explanations.49: This span with id='hasApi' will be filled in by JavaScript below to show whether the device motion API exists.
explanations.53: The requestPermission method is an iOS-specific way to ask users for motion sensor access; Android handles permissions differently.
explanations.63: Jerk is a physics term meaning how quickly acceleration changes — a sudden shake produces high jerk values.
explanations.88: This checks if the browser supports the Permissions API before trying to use it, since older browsers don't have it.
explanations.108: This sets a 3-second timer that will warn the user if no motion events arrive, meaning the sensor is blocked or unavailable.
explanations.119: Once a motion event arrives, we cancel that warning timer since we now know the sensor is working.
explanations.124: accelerationIncludingGravity gives you acceleration values that include Earth's gravity (9.8 m/s²), not just user movement.
explanations.136: Destructuring extracts x, y, and z from the acceleration object so we can use them as standalone variables.
explanations.145: Jerk is calculated as the sum of absolute changes in each axis, divided by the time elapsed, then multiplied by 1000 to convert to per-second units.
